title: Local existence and codimension calculus for dimension functions
statement: Let $T$ be a Noetherian universally catenary scheme, meaning that every affine coordinate ring is Noetherian and every finite-type algebra over it is catenary in the bounded saturated-chain sense of [def-exc-excellent-ring]. A dimension function is a function $\delta:|T|\to\mathbf Z$ such that $\delta(v)-\delta(w)=1$ for every immediate geometric specialization $\bar v\rightsquigarrow\bar w$; immediate means that the reduced closure of $\bar v$ in $T_{(\bar w)}$ has Krull dimension one [def-weil-geometric-point, def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit, def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. Dimension functions exist Zariski locally on $T$; in particular a Noetherian universally catenary local scheme admits one on the whole scheme. For any dimension function $\delta$ and any geometric specialization $\bar v\rightsquigarrow\bar w$, one has $\delta(v)-\delta(w)=c_T(\bar v,\bar w)$, where $c_T$ is the Krull dimension of that reduced closure in $T_{(\bar w)}$. This equality also holds for identity specializations and geometric isomorphisms, with codimension zero.

source.place: Expose XIV, Proposition 2.1.4, Theorem 2.2.1, Corollary 2.2.4 and proof of Lemma 2.2.5, printed pp.210–213: local existence and computation of codimension by differences.

proof.text: Work on an affine neighbourhood $\operatorname{Spec}R$ of a chosen point $x$, represented by a prime $\mathfrak q_x$. For comparable primes $\mathfrak p\subseteq\mathfrak q$, let $\ell(\mathfrak p,\mathfrak q)$ be the common length of saturated chains between them (zero when equal). This is a finite nonnegative integer: the catenary hypothesis in the cited definition bounds all finite chain lengths, so a chain of greatest length exists and is saturated. For $\mathfrak p\subseteq\mathfrak r\subseteq\mathfrak q$, concatenate greatest-length chains in the two intervals; their concatenation is saturated, hence $\ell(\mathfrak p,\mathfrak q)=\ell(\mathfrak p,\mathfrak r)+\ell(\mathfrak r,\mathfrak q)$. This is just the bounded saturated-chain definition, without an equidimensionality assumption on $R$.

source.place: Expose XIV, proof of Proposition 2.2.2; catenary chain calculation expanded as in Stacks algebra.tex, Tags 00NI (definition-catenary) and 00NL (definition-universally-catenary).

proof.text: The finite-components statement applied to this affine scheme and to each closed intersection of its irreducible components gives finite decompositions $\operatorname{Spec}R=\bigcup_i Z_i$ and $Z_i\cap Z_j=\bigcup_k W_{ijk}$. Components of an affine spectrum are $V(\mathfrak p_i)$ for minimal primes $\mathfrak p_i$, and sobriety supplies a generic prime $\mathfrak r_{ijk}$ for each irreducible closed $W_{ijk}=V(\mathfrak r_{ijk})$. Delete all $Z_i$ not containing $x$ and all $W_{ijk}$ not containing $x$. Their union is a finite closed set avoiding $x$, so its complement $U$ is an open neighbourhood of $x$. A surviving $Z_i$ has $\mathfrak p_i\subseteq\mathfrak q_x$. Put $a_i=\ell(\mathfrak p_i,\mathfrak q_x)$ and, for $y\in Z_i\cap U$ represented by $\mathfrak q_y$, put $\delta_i(y)=a_i-\ell(\mathfrak p_i,\mathfrak q_y)$. These are actual integer-valued functions, each normalized to zero at $x$.

source.place: Tag 02IC, lemma-locally-dimension-function, finite closed-component deletion construction; compare ILO XIV, Corollary 2.2.4.

proof.text:
If $y\in Z_i\cap Z_j\cap U$, choose $W_{ijk}$ containing $y$. It was not deleted, hence contains $x$. Write $\mathfrak r=\mathfrak r_{ijk}$; then both $\mathfrak q_y$ and $\mathfrak q_x$ contain $\mathfrak r$, and both $\mathfrak p_i$ and $\mathfrak p_j$ lie in $\mathfrak r$. The additivity proved in step 1 gives
$$\delta_i(y)=\ell(\mathfrak r,\mathfrak q_x)-\ell(\mathfrak r,\mathfrak q_y)=\delta_j(y).$$
Thus the $\delta_i$ define one function $\delta:U\to\mathbf Z$. For a Zariski immediate specialization $y\rightsquigarrow z$ in $U$, choose a component $Z_i$ containing $y$; it contains $z$ since it is closed. The prime interval from $\mathfrak q_y$ to $\mathfrak q_z$ is saturated and has length one: any intermediate prime would give a generalization of $z$, and so belongs to the open $U$. Step 1 gives $\delta(y)-\delta(z)=1$.

source.place: Tag 02IC, lemma-locally-dimension-function, displayed comparison through Z_{ijk}; omitted final verification written out using Tag 02I6, lemma-catenary-in-codimension.

proof.text: Let $\bar v\rightsquigarrow\bar w$ be an immediate geometric specialization on $U$; as $U\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq T$ are open, $U_{(\bar w)}=(\operatorname{Spec}R)_{(\bar w)}=T_{(\bar w)}$. Its underlying points are distinct: if $v=w$, the image point $p$ of $\bar v$ in $T_{(\bar w)}$ lies in the fibre over $w$, which is discrete by the discrete-fibre statement and contains the closed point $m$ (strict-localization functoriality); since $m\in\overline{\{p\}}$, discreteness of the fibre forces $p=m$, whose closure is one point, of dimension $0\neq1$. So $v\ne w$. Apply the geometric-immediate comparison to $X=\operatorname{Spec}R$: it is Noetherian (one affine chart), and each of its affine opens is an affine open of $T$, hence has universally catenary ring by the hypothesis on $T$. Its last assertion says that $\mathfrak q_v\subset\mathfrak q_w$ is saturated in $R$, so no point of $\operatorname{Spec}R$, in particular none of $U$, lies strictly between: $v\rightsquigarrow w$ is a Zariski immediate specialization in $U$. By step 3, $\delta(v)-\delta(w)=1$: the function constructed in steps 1–3 is a dimension function on $U$. This proves Zariski local existence in the stated sense. If $T$ is local, apply the construction at its closed point. An open neighbourhood of the closed point is the whole local scheme: in $\operatorname{Spec}A$, a basic neighbourhood $D(f)$ of its maximal ideal has $f$ a unit. Therefore the resulting dimension function is defined on all of $T$.

source.place: Expose XIV, Proposition 2.1.4 and Corollary 2.2.4; local-scheme conclusion by the unit criterion for basic opens.

proof.text: Now let $\delta$ be any dimension function on $T$ and fix a geometric point $\bar w$. Put $u:H=T_{(\bar w)}\to T$. The affine strict-local comparison identifies $H$ with the spectrum of the algebraic strict henselization of $\mathcal O_{T,w}$. The affine stalk-localization and Noetherian-localization statements make $\mathcal O_{T,w}$ Noetherian, and preservation of Noetherianity by strict henselization makes $H=\operatorname{Spec}B$ Noetherian local. Its closed point maps to $w$, by strict-localization functoriality. The affine-chart lemma makes $u$ ind-etale, and the strict-local invariance statement therefore identifies $H_{(\bar b)}$ with $T_{(u\bar b)}$ over $T$ for every geometric point $\bar b$ of $H$. The structural-map equality in the affine comparison and the over-$T$ equality in invariance ensure these are the actual structural maps, not just abstract isomorphisms of rings.

source.place: Expose XIV, Definition 2.1.8, paragraph on etale pullback of dimension functions; strict-local realization via Stacks more-algebra.tex Tag 06LJ and algebra.tex Tags 05WR and 0GIP (ind-etale strict-local invariance).

proof.text: For a Zariski immediate specialization $a\rightsquigarrow b$ in $H$, the local ring at $b$ of the reduced closure of $a$ has dimension one: its generalization chains correspond exactly to the chains between $a$ and $b$, so the stalk-dimension statement gives dimension one. The reduced-closed-subscheme statement supplies this closure as a scheme. Now the forward direction (a) of the immediate-specialization criterion, which requires only Noetherianity, says that every point over $a$ in $H_{(\bar b)}$ has one-dimensional closure. There is at least one such point by the nonempty-fibre assertion for strict localization. Choose a geometric point above it. Under the over-$T$ isomorphism $H_{(\bar b)}\simeq T_{(u\bar b)}$ of step 5, its image defines an immediate geometric specialization in $T$, with underlying endpoints $u(a),u(b)$. The geometric-specialization description is the map from a geometric point into the target strict localization. Thus $\delta(u(a))-\delta(u(b))=1$. In particular $\epsilon=\delta\circ u$ drops by one on every Zariski immediate specialization in $H$. No universal catenarity of $H$, no branch equidimensionality theorem, and no assumed dimension function on $H$ have been used in this argument.

source.place: Expose XIV, Definitions 2.1.1–2.1.2 and paragraph after Definition 2.1.8; pullback to the strict localization using the isomorphism of step 5.

proof.text:
Let the given specialization $\bar v\rightsquigarrow\bar w$ have image point $p\in H$, and let $m$ be the closed point of $H=\operatorname{Spec}B$. The closure $C=\overline{\{p\}}_{\mathrm{red}}$ is $\operatorname{Spec}(B/P)$, where $P$ is the prime of $p$: this is the reduced closed-subscheme construction, since a prime ideal is radical, and the quotient-spectrum homeomorphism. The finite Krull dimension of the Noetherian local ring $B$ bounds the lengths of all prime chains between $P$ and its maximal ideal. Hence a chain of greatest length $d$ between these endpoints exists. Any prime chain in $V(P)$ extends to these endpoints, so $d=\dim C$ by the quotient-spectrum identification and the equality of ring and topological Krull dimensions. A greatest-length chain is saturated. Telescope step 6 along its $d$ inclusions to obtain
$$\delta(v)-\delta(w)=\epsilon(p)-\epsilon(m)=d=\dim C=c_T(\bar v,\bar w).$$
When the underlying endpoints coincide, the strict-local fibre is discrete and contains $m$. Since $H$ is local, every point specializes to $m$, so a point of that fibre must equal $m$. Its closure is one point and $d=0$. This includes identity specializations and geometric isomorphisms, and proves all the zero-codimension clauses.

lean.statement: theorem local_dimension_function_calculus {T : Scheme.{u}} [IsNoetherian T] (hcat : ∀ U : T.affineOpens, IsUniversallyCatenary Γ(T, U)) : (∀ x : T, ∃ U : T.Opens, x ∈ U ∧ ∃ δ : U.toScheme → ℤ, Scheme.IsGeometricDimensionFunction U.toScheme δ) ∧ ((∃ (R : CommRingCat.{u}) (_ : IsLocalRing R), Nonempty (T ≅ Spec R)) → ∃ δ : T → ℤ, Scheme.IsGeometricDimensionFunction T δ) ∧ (∀ (δ : T → ℤ), Scheme.IsGeometricDimensionFunction T δ → ∀ (p q : StrictGeometricPoint T) (a : p ⟶ q), ∃ n : ℕ, StrictGeometricPoint.codimension a = (n : WithBot ℕ∞) ∧ δ p.underlying - δ q.underlying = (n : ℤ)) ∧ (∀ (p : StrictGeometricPoint T), StrictGeometricPoint.codimension (𝟙 p) = 0) ∧ (∀ (p q : StrictGeometricPoint T) (e : p ≅ q), StrictGeometricPoint.codimension e.hom = 0)
